# MATERIALS AND METHODS

## Particle Identification Procedure of AIM-MP

A key decision of the AIM-MP pipeline is to use a dedicated object detection stage before segmentation, rather than relying on a segmentation model alone. Segmentation models are effective at drawing pixel-wise masks, but they were designed to expect input prompts, whether from a click, a tap, or a bounding box. When applied to microscopy images without explicit prompts, the segmentation model's automatic mask generator tended to miss certain particles altogether while merging other distinct particles together, especially when particles appeared in close proximity. We therefore needed a reliable method to localize regions of interest before running the segmentation model. This motivated the development of a two-stage pipeline consisting of an object detection stage followed by a segmentation stage.

The object detection stage utilizes a custom-tuned YOLO11-Large architecture (25.3 M parameters, 86.6 GFLOPs) initialized from COCO-pretrained weights and fine-tuned on a custom labeled dataset to localize potential regions of interest. The segmentation stage utilizes Meta's native SAM 2 pretrained segmentation model to draw pixel-wise masks for individual microplastics and aggregates. The YOLO detection stage identifies bounding boxes containing a region of interest in the image. These bounding boxes are then passed as spatial prompts to the SAM 2 layer, which creates a single pixel-level mask for each YOLO prompt. This design allows the pipeline to exploit the strengths of each model while mitigating their respective limitations: YOLO provides domain-adapted localization with high recall, and SAM 2 contributes precise boundary delineation that would be difficult to achieve with YOLO's native bounding-box outputs alone.

## Dataset Preparation and Image Augmentation

Microplastic samples were collected from Lake Mendota (Madison, WI, USA), prepared on membrane filters, and imaged under 532 nm laser illumination using darkfield optical microscopy. A total of 78 darkfield microscopy images were manually annotated with bounding boxes encompassing two morphological classes---pellet and aggregate---following the YOLO format, with each image accompanied by a label file containing class indices and normalized bounding-box coordinates. The annotated dataset was partitioned into a training set of 64 images, a validation set of 8 images, and a held-out test set of 7 images (approximately 82%/10%/9%). The training--validation split was used for model optimization and hyperparameter selection, while the test set was reserved for final evaluation to assess generalization to unseen data.

Because darkfield microscopy images encode particle identity through spectral contrast and color intensity, no color-space augmentation (HSV hue, saturation, or value jitter) was applied during training, as distorting these channels would corrupt the very features the model must learn to distinguish. Instead, a suite of microscopy-appropriate geometric augmentations was employed. Full 360-degree random rotation was enabled, since microplastic samples deposited on membrane filters have no canonical orientation. Horizontal and vertical flipping were each applied with 50\% probability. Mild scale jitter ($\pm$25\%) and slight translational shift (10\% of the image dimension) introduced spatial variance without altering particle morphology. A light mixup augmentation (5\% probability) was included to regularize training. Mosaic augmentation was explicitly disabled to preserve the spatial context of particles on the substrate, as stitching four images together would create artificial particle arrangements and densities not representative of real samples. Copy--paste augmentation was also disabled, as it is not meaningful for bounding-box-only training. In addition to these explicit augmentations, Ultralytics automatically applied a lightweight Albumentations pipeline consisting of Blur ($p = 0.01$), MedianBlur ($p = 0.01$), ToGray ($p = 0.01$), and CLAHE ($p = 0.01$).

Over the course of training, the model completed 977 epochs before early stopping was triggered. At each epoch, all 64 training images were presented with independently sampled augmentations, and the 8 validation images were evaluated without augmentation. This amounts to $977 \times 64 = 62{,}528$ augmented training image presentations and $977 \times 8 = 7{,}816$ validation evaluations, yielding a total of approximately 70,344 image presentations seen by the model during the entire training process.

## Object Detection Model Training and Performance

The object detection stage utilized a YOLO11-Large architecture (25.3 M parameters, 86.6 GFLOPs) initialized from COCO-pretrained weights (1,009 of 1,015 weight tensors transferred) and fine-tuned on the microplastic dataset. The Large variant was selected as a deliberate trade-off between model capacity and inference speed: smaller YOLO variants (Nano, Small) lacked the representational depth needed to distinguish faint, low-contrast particles from substrate texture in darkfield images, while the Extra-Large variant offered marginal accuracy gains at substantially higher computational cost without justification given the relatively small number of object classes (two).

Training was conducted at an input resolution of $1280 \times 1280$ pixels---double the YOLO default of 640---because the microplastic particles of interest span only tens of pixels at native resolution. Reducing the input to 640 pixels caused the model to miss smaller particles entirely, as their spatial extent fell below the effective receptive field of the detection head. The elevated resolution preserves fine-grained particle morphology at the cost of higher memory consumption, which was accommodated by a batch size of 8 on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU (143 GB VRAM) provisioned through the Center for High Throughput Computing (CHTC) at the University of Wisconsin--Madison.

The model was trained using the AdamW optimizer rather than the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) optimizer that is conventional for YOLO training. AdamW was chosen because of the extremely small training set (64 images): its per-parameter adaptive learning rates help the model converge more stably when gradient estimates are noisy due to limited data diversity, whereas SGD's fixed momentum can cause erratic weight updates under these conditions. The initial learning rate was set to $1.5 \times 10^{-3}$---an order of magnitude below the typical YOLO default of $10^{-2}$---to prevent the fine-tuning process from overwriting the useful low-level feature representations inherited from COCO pretraining. Cosine annealing reduced the learning rate to a final fraction of 0.01 ($1.5 \times 10^{-5}$ effective), and a weight decay of 0.01 provided L2 regularization. A 5-epoch linear warm-up was applied to stabilize early gradient flow before the full learning rate was reached. Automatic mixed precision (AMP) was enabled to halve memory usage for activations and accelerate matrix operations on the H200's tensor cores without measurable loss in convergence quality.

Early stopping with a patience of 200 epochs halted training at epoch 977 (best weights saved at epoch 777), with the full run completing in approximately 0.57 hours of wall-clock time. The generous patience window of 200 epochs---significantly larger than the commonly used 50---was chosen because the small training set produces high-variance validation metrics from epoch to epoch, and premature stopping would risk discarding a model that had not yet fully converged. The 200-epoch gap between the best checkpoint and the stopping point confirms that the model had reached a genuine performance plateau rather than a transient fluctuation.

On the held-out validation set (8 images, 123 annotated instances), the best model achieved an overall precision of 89.3\%, recall of 96.1\%, mAP@50 of 95.3\%, and mAP@50-95 of 64.1\%. Per-class performance was as follows: for the pellet class, precision reached 99.2\% with an mAP@50 of 97.9\%, while the aggregate class attained 97.2\% recall and an mAP@50 of 92.8\%. The lower mAP@50-95 relative to mAP@50 is expected for this task, as microplastic bounding boxes are inherently imprecise---particles have irregular, non-rectangular boundaries, so even a well-localized box will not achieve tight overlap at the stringent IoU thresholds (0.75--0.95) used in the mAP@50-95 average. This limitation is precisely why the pipeline delegates precise boundary delineation to the downstream SAM 2 segmentation stage rather than relying on YOLO's bounding boxes alone. Inference speed was 4.3 ms per image, enabling near-real-time processing of large image batches.

During inference, a confidence threshold of 0.1 was applied---substantially lower than the conventional default of 0.25 or 0.5---because the pipeline prioritizes recall over precision at the detection stage. A missed particle (false negative) cannot be recovered by downstream segmentation, whereas a spurious detection (false positive) produces only a small mask on background substrate that is easily filtered during manual review or automated post-processing. Agnostic non-maximum suppression (NMS) was applied at an IoU threshold of 0.25 to eliminate duplicate overlapping detections regardless of predicted class. Class-agnostic NMS was necessary because pellet and aggregate particles can physically overlap or abut one another in the microscopy field of view; standard per-class NMS would allow two overlapping boxes of different classes to survive even when they refer to the same physical object, inflating the detection count. The relatively strict IoU threshold of 0.25---below the typical default of 0.45--0.7---was chosen to aggressively suppress near-duplicate detections in dense particle fields, where YOLO may propose multiple slightly offset boxes for a single particle.

## Instance Segmentation with SAM 2

Each bounding box produced by the YOLO detection stage was passed as a spatial prompt to the Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM 2), a vision-foundation model pre-trained on the SA-V dataset for promptable image and video segmentation. SAM 2 was loaded from the Hiera-Large checkpoint (sam2.1\_hiera\_large.pt) with its default configuration and deployed on GPU using the native `sam2` Python library. Prior to prompting, each YOLO bounding box was contracted inward by 10\% of its width and height to remove background margin pixels that would otherwise degrade mask quality; coordinates were clamped to image bounds to prevent box collapse. SAM 2 was run in single-mask mode for each box prompt independently: the image encoder processed the full-resolution image once per image, and the lightweight mask decoder was invoked once per bounding box, producing a logit map at full image resolution that was binarized at a threshold of 0.5 to obtain a pixel-precise segmentation mask. Because SAM 2 is a general-purpose segmentation model rather than a domain-specific classifier, it does not require any additional fine-tuning on microplastic imagery---its strong zero-shot transfer capability, when conditioned on YOLO-provided bounding boxes, produces high-quality masks that tightly conform to particle boundaries. This zero-shot approach eliminates the need for labor-intensive pixel-level annotation, which would be prohibitive for the irregularly shaped particles encountered in environmental microscopy. The resulting per-particle binary masks were composited onto the original image with a semi-transparent overlay ($\alpha = 0.45$) for visual inspection and exported alongside the original detection coordinates for downstream quantification.

## Rationale for Two-Stage Detection and Segmentation

A key design decision of the AIM-MP pipeline is the use of a dedicated object detection stage prior to segmentation, rather than relying on SAM 2 alone. Although SAM 2 is a powerful foundation model capable of producing high-quality segmentation masks, it was designed as a promptable segmentation model and does not perform object detection or classification on its own. When applied to a microscopy image without spatial prompts, SAM 2's automatic mask generator tends to over-segment the background substrate, merging particles with surface artifacts, or under-segment dense particle fields by grouping adjacent particles into a single mask. These failure modes are particularly pronounced in darkfield microscopy, where bright halos, substrate grain boundaries, and out-of-focus luminescent regions can be visually similar to microplastic particles. SAM 2 has no domain-specific knowledge of what constitutes a microplastic; it segments regions of visual coherence without discriminating between target particles and background features. In contrast, the YOLO detection model was fine-tuned specifically on annotated microplastic images and learns to localize particles based on morphological and spectral features characteristic of the domain. By first identifying candidate particle locations with YOLO and then passing each bounding box as a focused spatial prompt to SAM 2, the pipeline confines SAM 2's segmentation to regions that are already highly likely to contain a particle. This two-stage approach leverages the complementary strengths of each model: YOLO provides domain-adapted detection with high recall, while SAM 2 contributes precise boundary delineation that would be difficult to achieve with YOLO's native bounding-box or polygon outputs alone.
